# [Models]{.fg-pink}, [Harnesses]{.fg-green}, and [Tools]{.fg-yellow}

## Load the packages, as always

```{r}
#| label: "12-llms-01"
#| message: TRUE
library(here)      # manage file paths
library(socviz)    # data and some useful functions
library(tidyverse) # your friend and mine
library(btw)       # describe R things to LLMs
```

## Overview

1. What a Large Language Model actually is
2. The difference between the [**model**]{.fg-pink} and its [**harness**]{.fg-green}
3. [**Tools**]{.fg-blue}, and why they make the output better
4. [**Subscription**]{.fg-lblue} vs [**API**]{.fg-orange} access
5. Bringing R to the LLM with `btw`
6. Working with agents safely

# The [Model]{.fg-pink}

## What an LLM is

- A very large function: [text in]{.fg-lblue}, [text out]{.fg-green}
- Strictly, _tokens_ in, a probability distribution over the _next_ token out. Sample one, append it, repeat.
- Trained on an enormous amount of text (including a great deal of R code), then tuned to follow instructions and hold a conversation.
- Its weights are fixed after training. Its knowledge stops at a _training cutoff_.

## What an LLM is [not]{.fg-red}

On its own, the model _cannot_:

- Run code
- Look anything up
- Read your files
- Know today's date
- Remember your last conversation
- Learn anything, in the sense we usually use that word.

When a chat app seems to do these things, the work is being done [outside the model]{.fg-blue}.

## The model as a web API

You send a JSON request:

```{.json}
POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages

{
  "model": "claude-...",
  "max_tokens": 1024,
  "system": "You are a helpful assistant.",
  "messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content": "What's the median of 3, 5, 10, and 12?"}
  ]
}
```

## The model as a web API

And you get JSON back:

```{.json}
{
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": [
    {"type": "text", "text": "The median is 7.5."}
  ],
  "stop_reason": "end_turn",
  "usage": {"input_tokens": 31, "output_tokens": 9}
}
```

Note the `usage` field. Tokens are the unit of both [cost]{.fg-orange} and [capacity]{.fg-orange}.

## It is [stateless]{.fg-pink}

- The model keeps no record of the conversation between requests.
- So every request has to carry the [_whole conversation so far_]{.fg-green}.
- The "Pachinko Machine" picture.
- The "memory" in a chat window is just the prior turns being re-sent each time.
- Consequences:
  - Long conversations cost more per message, and get slower.
  - There is a hard ceiling: the _context window_.
  - Quality degrades as the context fills up with irrelevant material.

## Some vocabulary

- [**Turn**]{.fg-lblue}: one message, from either the user or the assistant.
- [**Context**]{.fg-lblue}: everything sent to the model in a single request: system prompt, prior turns, tool definitions, tool results.
- [**Tool**]{.fg-lblue}: a function the model can _ask_ to have run.
- [**Round**]{.fg-lblue}: everything that happens between your request and the final answer. Possibly many turns.

## The model alone is [confidently wrong]{.fg-red} about some things

Ask a bare model, with no tools, to multiply two eight-digit numbers.

It will produce a number. The number will have the right number of digits, and the right first few digits. It will look entirely plausible.

```{r}
#| label: "12-llms-02"
x <- 20598162
y <- 83106206

format(x * y, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
```

One bare model answered `1,711,067,239,026,172`, which is close but wrong.

## Why the model gets this wrong

- The model produces _plausible continuations_. For arithmetic on numbers it has never seen, plausible is not the same as correct.
- The same thing happens with R code:
  - Arguments that don't exist, or that used to exist
  - Superseded idioms: `%>%`, `gather()`/`spread()`, `aes_string()`, `size` for line widths
  - Functions from packages newer than the training cutoff simply aren't known
- A better model helps less here than [giving the model a way to check its answer]{.fg-green}.

# The [Harness]{.fg-green}

## The model and the harness

- "Claude" the _app_ is not the same thing as "Claude" the _model_.
- A [**harness**]{.fg-green} is the program wrapped around the model. It:
  - Manages the conversation and re-sends it
  - Writes a system prompt
  - Reads context files from disk
  - Tells the model what tools exist
  - [_Runs_]{.fg-blue} the tools the model asks for
  - Enforces permissions
  - Gives you an interface

## Harnesses you may have met

- **claude.ai** and the Claude Desktop app
- **Claude Code**, in the terminal or inside an editor like VS Code or Positron
- Other coding agents: Codex, Gemini CLI, Positron Assistant, GitHub Copilot
- **ellmer**, an R package: your R session becomes the harness

The same underlying model behaves very differently in each, because the harness decides what the model sees and what it can do.

## Where things live

```{.markdown}
  You  <──────>  Harness  <──── JSON over HTTPS ────>  Model
                    ▲
                    │
                    ▼
          Tools: files, R, shell, web
```

- The [harness]{.fg-green} holds the system prompt, context files, conversation history, and tool definitions. It runs the tools.
- It may run on your machine (Claude Code, `ellmer`) or on a server (claude.ai).
- The [model]{.fg-pink} only ever receives text, and only ever returns text.
(A consequence of this: there is no more "secret", "underlying", or
"lower-level" language that "programmers" or Anthropic, or whomever, speak to
the model in. It's all just natural-language text top to bottom.)

## Who does what

| Component                            | Provided by |
|:-------------------------------------|:------------|
| Predicting the next token            | Model       |
| System prompt                        | Harness     |
| Re-sending earlier turns             | Harness     |
| Reading `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`     | Harness     |
| Describing the available tools        | Harness     |
| Actually running a tool               | Harness     |
| Asking you for permission             | Harness     |

Most of the differences you notice day to day are [harness]{.fg-green} differences.

## Context files are just text

This course's repository has an `AGENTS.md` file. Part of it:

```{.markdown}
# Constraints

- Some datasets used may be very large. Do NOT attempt to ingest them in
  order to inspect them. Use the available local tools (R and its packages;
  the package APIs that allow the data to be queried, your plugins and
  skills, etc). You may extract very small samples (<1000 rows) from data
  files if it's necessary.

- The user will handle git and other version control matters.
```

The harness pastes this into the context at the start of every session, which is how "project memory" works.

# [Tools]{.fg-yellow}

## What a tool is

- A function that the [harness]{.fg-green} runs on the [model's]{.fg-pink} behalf.
- The model sees only three things about it:
  1. A [name]{.fg-blue}
  2. A [description]{.fg-blue}, in plain English
  3. A [schema]{.fg-blue} for its arguments
- The model emits a structured request: "call `read_file` with `path = 'R/clean.R'`".
- The harness runs it and sends the result back as text, in the next request.

## Read tools and write tools

- [**Read tools**]{.fg-lblue} observe the world: list files, read a file, read a help page, describe a data frame, check `git status`.
- [**Write tools**]{.fg-orange} change the world: write or edit a file, run a shell command, make a commit.

## The loop

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as You
  participant H as Harness
  participant M as Model
  U->>H: "Plot donors by year for each country"
  H->>M: prompt + tool definitions
  M->>H: tool request: describe organdata
  H->>M: tool result: columns, types, ranges
  M->>H: tool request: run this ggplot code
  H->>M: tool result: error, no column 'donor'
  M->>H: tool request: run the corrected code
  H->>M: tool result: success
  M->>H: final answer
  H->>U: "Here's the plot ..."
```

## Agents

> An agent is an LLM, in a harness, that calls tools repeatedly in a loop.

The loop: [**read**]{.fg-lblue}, [**act**]{.fg-orange}, [**read again**]{.fg-lblue} to check what happened, decide what to do next.

::: aside
Hadley Wickham, "[What is an agent?](https://substack.hadley.nz/p/what-is-an-agent)"
:::

## A tool is just a function

Here's a calculator. It evaluates an expression in an environment that contains only arithmetic.

```{r}
#| label: "12-llms-03"
calculator <- function(code) {
  math_env <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
  ops <- c("+", "-", "*", "/", "^", "(", "sqrt", "exp", "log")
  walk(ops, \(op) assign(op, get(op, envir = baseenv()), envir = math_env))
  eval(parse(text = code), envir = math_env)
}

calculator("20598162 * 83106206") |>
  format(big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
```

## A tool is just a function

And because of how it's built, it can't do anything else:

```{r}
#| label: "12-llms-04"
#| error: TRUE
calculator("read.csv('secrets.csv')")
```

Give the model this tool, describe it as "_use this for any arithmetic, since you can't reliably compute it yourself_", and it gets the multiplication right.

## What the model sees of a tool

Here is one of the tools in the `btw` package, as the model receives it:

```{r}
#| label: "12-llms-05"
help_tool <- btw_tools("btw_tool_docs_help_page")[[1]]

help_tool@description

help_tool@arguments@properties |>
  map_chr(\(p) p@description) |>
  str_trunc(70)
```

That text is [_all_]{.fg-blue} the model knows about this tool, so the descriptions have to be written carefully.

## Why tools improve the output

1. [**Ground truth instead of plausible guesses.**]{.fg-green} A calculator. The help page for the version of `dplyr` _you actually have installed_.
2. [**Current information.**]{.fg-green} Today's date. Package release notes. The web.
3. [**Verification.**]{.fg-green} Run the code. Run the tests. Render the document. Look at the error. Try again.
4. [**Acting, not just suggesting.**]{.fg-green} Edit the file directly, instead of handing you a snippet to paste.

Of the four, verification matters most: a model that can check its own work is much more reliable than one that can't.

## Tools also [manage]{.fg-yellow} the output

- An **edit** tool that replaces one exact span of text fails and complains if the text isn't found. That's safer than having the model rewrite a whole file from memory.
- **Structured output**: constrain the response to some schema, so you get a data frame back, not prose.
- **Deterministic steps should use deterministic tools.** Don't ask a model to format code. Run `air format .`
- A context-file instruction ("_always run `air`_") is a request. A
[_hook_]{.fg-orange} that mechanically runs `air` every time a file is saved is
a much stronger guarantee.

## A coding agent is a handful of tools

1. Read a file
2. Write a file
3. Edit part of a file
4. List files
5. Search across files
6. Run a shell command

Only 1, 2, and 6 are strictly essential. Claude Code's built-in tools are essentially these, plus web search and fetch, and the ability to start sub-agents.

::: aside
Hadley Wickham, "[A coding agent is six functions in a trenchcoat](https://substack.hadley.nz/p/a-coding-agent-is-six-functions-in)"
:::

# [Subscription]{.fg-lblue} vs [API]{.fg-orange}

## Two ways to pay for the same models

|                | [Subscription]{.fg-lblue}                    | [API]{.fg-orange}                          |
|:---------------|:---------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| You pay        | A flat monthly fee                           | Per token, input and output                |
| Limits         | Usage caps that reset over time windows      | Rate limits, plus spend limits you set     |
| Credentials    | Log in with your account                     | An API key, e.g. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`       |
| Harness        | Anthropic's: claude.ai, Desktop, Claude Code | Anything: Claude Code, `ellmer`, your own  |
| Good for       | Interactive work                             | Programs, pipelines, batch jobs, apps      |

## API keys for your own code

- A subscription login is for use with the provider's own apps.
- If [_your_ code]{.fg-blue} calls the model directly, it needs an [API key]{.fg-orange}. That includes `ellmer::chat_anthropic()` and `btw::btw_client()`.
- API keys are secrets.
  - Keep them in `~/.Renviron`, never in a script. There are fancier ways to
  manage this too.
  - Never commit them to git.
  - Set a spend limit in the console.

## Two directions

[**Bring the LLM to R**]{.fg-orange}

- `ellmer` in your R session. R _is_ the harness.
- Needs an API key.
- Good for using an LLM as part of an analysis, e.g. classifying 10,000 open-ended survey responses.

[**Bring R to the LLM**]{.fg-lblue}

- An existing harness, like Claude Code, calls R through tools.
- Works with a subscription.
- Good for interactive work: writing, checking, and fixing code with your data and your packages.

## For reference: R as the harness

This needs an API key, so we won't run it today. The whole harness is about a dozen lines.

```{.r}
library(ellmer)

chat <- chat_anthropic()   # needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

chat$register_tool(tool(
  calculator,
  description = "Evaluate a mathematical expression. Use this for any
    arithmetic, since you can't reliably compute it yourself.",
  arguments = list(code = type_string("An expression, e.g. '1 + 2 * 3'."))
))

chat$chat("What's 20598162 * 83106206?")
#> ◯ [tool call] calculator(code = "20598162 * 83106206")
#> ● #> 1711835094393372
#> 20598162 × 83106206 = 1,711,835,094,393,372.
```

::: aside
After Hadley Wickham, "[Your LLM can't math (and that's ok)](https://substack.hadley.nz/p/your-llm-cant-math-and-thats-ok)"
:::

# [Bringing R to the LLM]{.fg-lblue}

## The Model Context Protocol (MCP)

- A standard way for a harness to discover and call tools provided by some other program.
- The harness is the MCP [**client**]{.fg-green}. The program providing tools is an MCP [**server**]{.fg-blue}.
- Write the server once and it works with any client: Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Positron, VS Code.
- If R can run an MCP server, any of these harnesses can use R as a tool.

## The `btw` package

"By the way, here's some context." A toolkit for describing R things to LLMs.

Three ways to use it:

1. [**`btw()`**]{.fg-blue} at the console: copies a description to the clipboard, for pasting into any chat.
2. [**`btw_mcp_server()`**]{.fg-blue}: serves R tools to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, etc.
3. [**`btw_client()`**]{.fg-blue}: an `ellmer` chat with `btw` tools. Needs an API key.

Modes 1 and 2 work with a subscription.

## Mode 1: `btw()` at the console

```{r}
#| label: "12-llms-06"
organ_small <- organdata |>
  select(country, year, donors, consent_law)

btw(organ_small, clipboard = FALSE)
```

Interactively, `btw(organ_small)` puts this on your clipboard, ready to paste into claude.ai.

## Mode 1: `btw()` at the console

You can mix objects, documentation, and your question:

```{.r}
btw(
  organ_small,
  dplyr::across,
  vignette("colwise", "dplyr"),
  "Using across(), get the mean and sd of every numeric column by consent_law."
)
#> ✔ btw copied to the clipboard!
```

- The model gets your [actual column names and types]{.fg-green}, not guesses.
- It gets the help page from [your installed version]{.fg-green} of `dplyr`.
- This is crude, but it works with any chat interface, and it's much better than giving the model no context.

## Mode 2: `btw` as an MCP server

Tell Claude Code about it, once, from the terminal:

```{.zsh}
claude mcp add -s user r-btw -- Rscript -e \
  "btw::btw_mcp_server(list('docs', 'env', 'sessioninfo', 'cran'))"
```

Check that it's connected:

```{.zsh}
claude mcp list
#> r-btw: Rscript -e btw::btw_mcp_server(...) - ✔ Connected
```

Now, in every Claude Code session, the model can call R's help system, inspect data frames, check installed packages, and search CRAN.

## Choosing tool groups

```{r}
#| label: "12-llms-07"
btw_tools() |>
  map(\(t) tibble(group = t@annotations$btw_group, tool = t@name)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  summarize(tools = n(), .by = group)
```

- Claude Code already has its own file, search, and shell tools. Don't duplicate them.
- `docs`, `env`, `sessioninfo`, and `cran` are a good start. Add `pkg` if you write packages.
- `btw_tool_run_r` is opt-in. Name it explicitly to let the model run R code.

## Docs in the loop

Ask a model about `purrr::in_parallel()`, added in mid-2025. Without tools, it may not know it exists, or may confidently invent arguments. With `btw`, it calls a tool instead:

:::{.smallcode}

```{r}
#| label: "12-llms-08"
help_lines <- btw_tool_docs_help_page("in_parallel", "purrr")@value |>
  str_split_1("\n")

help_lines[str_which(help_lines, "#### Usage"):length(help_lines)] |>
  head(16) |>
  writeLines()
```

:::

## Connecting to your [live]{.fg-yellow} R session

- By default, the MCP server runs in its own fresh R process. It can't see the objects in your console.
- To share your session, run this in your interactive R console (RStudio or Positron):

```{.r}
btw::btw_mcp_session()
```

- Now the `env` tools describe _your_ data frames, and `run_r` runs in _your_ session.
- The model calls `list_r_sessions` and `select_r_session` to find it.
- If Claude Code was already running, reconnect with `/mcp`.

## An interactive workflow

In your R console:

```{.r}
library(tidyverse)
library(socviz)

organ_small <- organdata |>
  select(country, year, donors, consent_law)

btw::btw_mcp_session()
```

In Claude Code:

```{.markdown}
Using `organ_small` in my R session, make a faceted line plot of donors
by year for each country, grouped by consent_law. Use current ggplot2
conventions. Run the code to check that it works before showing it to me.
```

## The tool calls, step by step

| Step | Tool call                               | What it does                                |
|:----:|:----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| 1    | `select_r_session`                       | Attaches to your console                    |
| 2    | `btw_tool_env_describe_data_frame`       | Real column names, types, ranges              |
| 3    | `btw_tool_docs_help_page` (`ggplot2`)    | Current arguments, e.g. `linewidth` not `size` |
| 4    | `btw_tool_run_r`                         | Runs the code; sees warnings and errors       |
| 5    | `btw_tool_run_r` (again)                 | Fixes the problem and re-checks               |
| 6    | _Final answer_                            | Code that has actually been run               |

The plot appears in your session's plot pane, because the code ran in _your_ session.

## Why this beats copy-and-paste

- [Documentation]{.fg-green} from the versions you have installed.
- [Data]{.fg-green}: actual names and types, without uploading the data itself.
- [Verification]{.fg-green}: code is run before you see it.
- [Iteration]{.fg-green}: you keep working in your console; the model works alongside it on the same objects.
- [Package work]{.fg-green}: with the `pkg` group, the model can `document()`, `test()`, and `check()` in the loop.

## The `btw` command-line tool

Some harnesses can't use MCP, or you want to keep tool definitions out of the context. `btw` also ships a CLI.

```{.r}
btw::install_btw_cli()
```

```{.zsh}
btw docs topics purrr
btw docs help dplyr::across
btw pkg test
```

Any agent with a shell tool can call it. The installer offers a _skill_ telling the agent the CLI exists.

## Context files and skills

- [**Context files**]{.fg-blue}: `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` at the root of a project. Standing instructions: style rules, project layout, things to avoid.
- [**Skills**]{.fg-blue}: folders of instructions (and sometimes scripts) that the harness loads only when relevant. Cheap until needed.
- R packages can ship skills. `btw_skill_install_package()` installs them; `btw_skill_install_project()` does it for all of a project's dependencies.
- Again, these are plain-text files. A skill is just a Markdown file full of
instructions written in English.
- Widely used skills can be kept in you `~/.claude` folder; the Agent knows how
to install them. Project-specific ones can be kept in the equivalent folder of
the project and versioned with git like everything else in it.

# Working [safely]{.fg-red}

## Agents act

- Acting on your behalf is what makes an agent useful, and it also means its
mistakes have real consequences. You're letting it use your computer.
- Harnesses offer [permission modes]{.fg-blue}: ask before every action; allow edits but ask about commands; plan only; or decide automatically.
- [Sandboxes]{.fg-blue} restrict which files and which network hosts a command can touch.

## "Auto" doesn't mean "careful"

Hadley Wickham asked two coding agents in auto mode to install a tool via `curl ... | sh`, i.e. run a script from the internet without reading it.

- Both recognized this was risky.
- Both ran it anyway, because the user had asked.
- One disabled its own sandbox when the sandbox got in the way.

The model's judgment is not an effective security device.

::: aside
"[Auto mode knows it's dangerous (and does it anyway)](https://substack.hadley.nz/p/auto-mode-knows-its-dangerous-and)"
:::

## What sort of data are you analyzing?

- Even with tool calls and local evaluation, you're still talking to a model
that is on someone else's computer, and not just code but also data may be
exchanged between you and it.

- Are you comfortable with this? Are you _permitted_ to do this? What are the
rules (licensing; IRB-related; MOUs; federal law ...) governing data sharing?
What are the terms under which you are using the Agent? Does the company providing
the agent assert the right to treat any communication with you as future
training data?

## Practical safeguards

- [**git is your safety net.**]{.fg-green} Commit before you let an agent
loose. Use basic branch discipline. Read the diff afterwards.
- Keep secrets out of reach. `.Renviron` for keys, not scripts.
- Large datasets: tell the agent to _query_ it (with `duckdb`, `arrow`,
`dbplyr`), not read it.
- Think about developing your code on dummy or synthetic data. There are a
number of useful R packages for this: `messy`, `faux`, `synthpop`, `charlatan`,
`missMethods`.
- Start with read-only tools. Add write tools as you gain confidence.
- Prefer narrow tools with simple inputs to "run anything".

## Implications for your work

- The model's output is a draft. [Your judgment]{.fg-blue} is the check. Also,
you are still responsible for everything.
- It's important to bear this in mind because you are definitely going to be
tempted to be lazy, and just tell the robot to do everything.
- Verification matters _more_ now, not less: tests, rendering, `targets` pipelines.
- An LLM's responses are not reproducible, but the code it writes is reproducible once you've read and committed it.
- The things this course has covered (plain text, the shell, scripts, Quarto, git, build systems, packages) are what make a project legible to an agent.
